To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

HIV-infected individuals with HCV co-infections have a high rate of fibrosis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinomas, and that HIV infection accelerates liver disease and HCV viremia in co-infected individuals.
HIV infection accelerates HCV-related disease progression and that HCV-related liver diseases can limit the ability of HIV-infected patients to receive anti-retroviral therapies.
HCV co-infections with HIV are common, and serious.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the pathogenesis of HCV infection and its complications, and developing new therapeutic approaches to HCV infection.
the molecular mechanisms underlying HCV replication, the pathogenesis of liver disease and the development of novel therapies to prevent HCV-induced liver disease.
the molecular mechanisms of HIV and hepatitis C virus replication, and the interaction of these viruses in co-infected patients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the presence of HIV and hepatitis C virus infection in the same individual results in a synergistic interaction that is more severe than that seen with either virus alone.
HIV/HCV co-infection represents a significant health care issue that is not being adequately addressed by current guidelines.
HIV/HCV co-infection results in a significant increase in morbidity and mortality.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
HCV infection accelerates the clinical course of liver disease in HIV-infected patients and that HIV infection may accelerate HCV-related disease.
HCV co-infections is a serious and common problem for people with HIV, and that physicians must be aware of the problem and address it.
HCV infection is an important cause of morbidity in HIV-infected patients.
The main takeaway from our work is that
HCV infection is a major problem in HIV-infected persons and that it should be treated aggressively.
HIV/HCV coinfected patients are at a high risk for HCC and should be screened regularly for this disease.
